questions.stem: At standard speed, how much time does one small box on EKG paper represent?
questions.why: Paper runs at 25 mm/second. Each small box is 1 mm wide — 0.04 seconds — and each large box is five of those, or 0.20 seconds. Five large boxes make one second.

options.t: 0.01 seconds, one hundredth of a second
options.why: That is finer than the standard grid resolves.

options.t: 0.20 seconds, the width of one large box
options.why: One large box holds five small boxes and does represent 0.20 seconds.

options.t: 0.10 seconds, half of one large box
options.why: Half a large box is two and a half small boxes, not one.

options.t: 0.04 seconds

questions.stem: What does one small box represent vertically on a properly calibrated tracing?
questions.why: Vertically, one small box is 1 mm, or 0.1 mV. The standard calibration pulse is 10 mm tall — 1 mV — and confirms the machine is set correctly before you measure anything.

options.t: 0.04 second, the same as horizontally
options.why: Horizontal measurement is time; the vertical axis is voltage.

options.t: 1 millivolt, which is the standard calibration pulse
options.why: 1 mV is ten small boxes tall — that is the calibration box itself, not a single square.

options.t: 0.1 millivolt
5 millimeters of amplitude
options.why: 5 mm is the height of a large box, which is five small ones.

questions.stem: A 12-lead shows a calibration mark half the usual height. What does that mean for your interpretation?
questions.why: Half standardization is sometimes used deliberately when tall complexes overlap. Amplitude-based findings — hypertrophy criteria, ST elevation — must be read against that halved scale.

options.t: Intervals are halved, so the QRS will look artificially narrow
options.why: Calibration affects the vertical scale only — timing is set by paper speed.

options.t: The heart rate will calculate out at half its true value
options.why: Rate comes from spacing along the horizontal axis, which is unchanged.

options.t: The tracing is unusable and has to be repeated before reading
options.why: It is still readable; you simply account for the scale when judging amplitude.

options.t: Voltages are halved, so amplitude criteria read low

questions.stem: What does the P wave represent?
questions.why: The P wave is the atria depolarizing. Its shape and its relationship to the QRS is where rhythm interpretation begins.

options.t: Atrial repolarization
options.why: Atrial repolarization is buried inside the QRS and is not normally visible.

options.t: Atrial depolarization
Ventricular repolarization
options.why: That is the T wave.

options.t: Ventricular depolarization
options.why: That is the QRS complex.

questions.stem: Why is atrial repolarization not normally visible on the EKG?
questions.why: Atrial repolarization produces a small wave that occurs at the same time as ventricular depolarization. The QRS is far larger and buries it.

options.t: It is hidden inside the much larger QRS complex
It occurs before the P wave and falls outside the tracing
options.why: Repolarization follows depolarization; it cannot precede its own P wave.

options.t: The atria do not repolarize between beats
options.why: Every depolarized tissue must repolarize before it can fire again.

options.t: Standard limb leads are not oriented to detect it
options.why: Lead orientation is not the issue — the signal is simply overwhelmed.

questions.stem: What is the normal PR interval, and what does it measure?
questions.why: The PR interval runs from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS — three to five small boxes. It is mostly AV nodal delay, so a long PR means the impulse is being held up at the junction.

options.t: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, from P onset to QRS onset
0.06 to 0.10 seconds, from P onset to P offset
options.why: That range and those landmarks describe the P wave itself.

options.t: 0.20 to 0.40 seconds, from QRS onset to T offset
options.why: That describes the QT interval.

options.t: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds, from P offset to QRS onset
options.why: The interval starts at the beginning of the P wave; from the P's end to the QRS is the PR segment.

questions.stem: Per the lecture's measurements, what QRS duration is still normal and what duration is called wide?
questions.why: The lecture draws the line between 0.11 and 0.12: up to 0.11 seconds — under three small boxes — is normal, and 0.12 or more is a wide complex. That single boundary is what separates supraventricular from ventricular origin on nearly every strip you will be asked to read.

options.t: Normal to 0.20 seconds; wide above 0.20
options.why: 0.20 is the upper limit of the PR interval, not the QRS.

options.t: Normal to 0.10 seconds; wide at 0.11 and above
options.why: 0.11 is still within normal here.

options.t: Normal to 0.11 seconds; wide at 0.12 and above
Normal to 0.12 seconds; wide above 0.12
options.why: 0.12 is the first wide value in this lecture, not the last normal one.

questions.stem: Why is the QT interval corrected for heart rate?
questions.why: Repolarization happens faster at faster rates, so a raw QT means little without the rate. QTc corrects for that — above roughly 0.44 to 0.46 seconds raises the risk of torsades.

options.t: Only the QRS portion varies with rate, not the T wave
options.why: The QRS is quite stable across rates; it is repolarization that shifts.

options.t: Rate changes the paper speed used to record it
options.why: Paper speed is fixed at 25 mm/second regardless of rate.

options.t: The QT shortens naturally as the rate rises
Correction converts millimeters into milliseconds
options.why: Millimeters convert to time by paper speed alone, at any rate.

questions.stem: There are four large boxes between two R waves. What is the rate?
questions.why: The sequence from one large box out is 300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50. Four large boxes lands on 75 — the same as 300 divided by 4.

options.why: 150 is two large boxes.
60 would be five large boxes apart.
100 corresponds to three large boxes.

questions.stem: Why does the six-second method suit an irregular rhythm better than the box method?
questions.why: In an irregular rhythm, no two R-R intervals match, so measuring one gives a rate that is not representative. Counting the complexes in six seconds and multiplying by ten averages the variation.

options.t: It averages several beats, not one interval
It is more precise for any rhythm, regular or not
options.why: For a regular rhythm the box method is the more precise of the two.

options.t: It measures atrial and ventricular rates at the same time
options.why: Either method can be applied to P waves or QRS complexes separately.

options.t: It works without a calibrated paper speed
options.why: It depends entirely on paper speed — that is how you know the strip is six seconds long.

questions.stem: You count 9 QRS complexes across a six-second strip. What is the ventricular rate?
questions.why: Six seconds is one tenth of a minute, so multiply the count by ten: 9 × 10 = 90 per minute.

options.why: That halves the count before multiplying, which no method calls for.
That multiplies by six rather than ten; a six-second strip is a tenth of a minute.
That would be twelve complexes in six seconds, not nine.

questions.stem: Where does V1 go?
questions.why: V1 sits in the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border and V2 mirrors it on the left. Getting V1 and V2 too high is the most common placement error and can fake an anterior infarct pattern.

options.t: Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
options.why: That is V2 — V1 and V2 straddle the sternum at the same level.

options.t: Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line
options.why: That is V4.

options.t: Second intercostal space, right sternal border
options.why: That is where you would auscultate the aortic area, not place V1.

questions.stem: Which precordial lead is placed first when you work left to right, and why does its position matter to the rest?
questions.why: After V1 and V2, place V4 at the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line. V3 goes midway between V2 and V4, and V5 and V6 follow V4's horizontal level.

options.t: V6, because it anchors the midaxillary line
options.why: V6 is placed after V4 and V5, at the same level V4 established.

options.t: V1, because every other lead is measured from the sternum
options.why: V1 and V2 are placed first, but V3 is positioned between V2 and V4, so V4 has to exist first.

options.t: V4, because V3 and V5 are then set relative to it
V5, because it sits at the anterior axillary line
options.why: V5 is placed between V4 and V6, so it also depends on V4.

questions.stem: Which leads look at the inferior wall?
questions.why: Leads II, III and aVF face the inferior wall — usually right coronary territory. Septal is V1–V2, anterior V3–V4, lateral V5–V6 with I and aVL.

options.t: I and aVL
options.why: I and aVL look at the high lateral wall.

options.t: V1 and V2, the septal leads
options.why: V1 and V2 look at the septum, not the inferior wall.

options.t: V3 and V4
options.why: V3 and V4 look at the anterior wall.

options.t: II, III, and aVF

questions.stem: What is the point of placing lead V4R?
questions.why: V4R is V4's mirror position on the right chest. ST elevation there means right ventricular infarct, which changes management — that patient is preload-dependent and nitroglycerin can drop their pressure sharply.

options.t: To improve the tracing quality when V4 shows artifact
options.why: Artifact is fixed by prepping the skin and securing the cable, not by moving the lead.

options.t: To confirm posterior wall involvement behind the heart
options.why: Posterior involvement is checked with V7 through V9, or read as reciprocal changes in V1–V3.

options.t: To replace V4 when the left chest cannot be accessed
options.why: A mirror-image placement is not a substitute reading of the same wall.

options.t: To look at the right ventricle in an inferior MI

questions.stem: A monitor shows a flat line in one limb lead while other leads look normal. What should you check first?
questions.why: A rhythm that appears in some leads but not others is an equipment problem. Asystole must always be confirmed in more than one lead before it is treated as asystole.

options.t: Whether the patient has gone into asystole
options.why: Asystole appears in every lead at once, not one.

options.t: The patient's pulse and level of consciousness
options.why: Worth doing on any alarm, but a single flat lead among normal ones is an electrode problem.

options.t: The machine's calibration setting
options.why: Miscalibration scales all leads together rather than nulling one.

options.t: That electrode and its cable connection

questions.stem: A tracing shows a fine, regular tremor across the baseline in every lead at about 60 cycles per second. What is the likely cause?
questions.why: Sixty-cycle interference comes from AC power sources. Move away from the source or unplug what you can — the frequency is the giveaway, since 60 per second is far too fast to be physiologic.

options.t: Patient shivering or muscle tremor
options.why: Muscle artifact is coarse and irregular rather than a uniform 60-cycle pattern.

options.t: Atrial flutter waves being picked up as noise
options.why: Flutter waves are a cardiac signal at roughly 300 per minute, not 60 per second.

options.t: Electrical interference from nearby AC power
A loose electrode losing contact intermittently
options.why: A loose electrode produces wandering baseline or dropout in one lead.

questions.stem: Working through a rhythm strip systematically, what should you determine first?
questions.why: The usual order is regularity, then rate, then P waves, then PR interval, then QRS width. Answering those five in sequence names almost every rhythm you will see.

options.t: What the patient's blood pressure is
options.why: The patient always comes first clinically, but this question is about reading the strip.

options.t: Whether the axis is deviated
options.why: Axis requires a 12-lead and does not bear on identifying the rhythm.

options.t: Whether the rhythm is regular
Whether ST segments are elevated
options.why: ST analysis belongs to a 12-lead, not to rhythm interpretation on a monitor strip.

questions.stem: Every P wave is followed by a QRS, and every QRS is preceded by a P. What does that tell you?
questions.why: One-for-one conduction tells you the atria and ventricles are linked, but not where the impulse started or how long conduction took. P wave shape and PR duration answer those.

options.t: The rhythm must be normal sinus
options.why: One-for-one conduction happens in sinus tachycardia and bradycardia too, and in some atrial rhythms.

options.t: The atria and ventricles conduct one-for-one
The impulse definitely started in the SA node
options.why: A low atrial or junctional focus can also conduct one-for-one; P wave morphology is what points to origin.

options.t: No AV block of any degree is present
options.why: First-degree block conducts every P and still counts as a block.

questions.stem: What does an inverted P wave just before a narrow QRS in lead II suggest?
questions.why: Normal atrial depolarization runs toward lead II's positive electrode and makes an upright P. An impulse starting low travels backward through the atria, inverting the P in lead II.

options.t: The electrodes on the arms have been reversed
options.why: Limb lead reversal inverts the QRS along with the P wave; here the QRS is unremarkable.

options.t: A ventricular focus is driving the rhythm
options.why: A ventricular focus produces a wide QRS, and this one is narrow.

options.t: The impulse started low in the atria or junction
The atria are depolarizing after the ventricles
options.why: A P wave preceding the QRS means the atria fired first.

questions.stem: Leads I and aVF are both upright. What does that indicate about axis?
questions.why: The quick two-lead check: both upright is normal. I up with aVF down is left, I down with aVF up is right, and both down is the extreme quadrant.

options.t: Extreme axis deviation
options.why: Extreme deviation, sometimes called northwest axis, has both leads negative.

options.t: Left axis deviation
options.why: Left axis deviation shows lead I upright with aVF negative.

options.t: Normal axis
Right axis deviation
options.why: Right axis deviation shows lead I negative with aVF upright.

questions.stem: What is the most reliable way to reduce muscle and movement artifact before recording a 12-lead?
questions.why: Dry the skin, clip excess hair, place electrodes over bone rather than muscle where you can, and get the patient still and warm. Every downstream measurement depends on a clean baseline.

options.t: Increase the gain so the complexes stand out from the noise
options.why: Raising gain amplifies the artifact along with the signal.

options.t: Record a longer strip and pick the cleanest section
options.why: Averaging over time does not fix a signal that is noisy throughout.

options.t: Switch the monitor into diagnostic filtering mode
options.why: Diagnostic mode widens the filter and lets more artifact through, not less.

options.t: Prep the skin and get the patient still

questions.stem: Where is the J point, and why does it matter?
questions.why: The J point is the junction of the QRS and the ST segment. ST elevation and depression are measured there, against the TP or PR segment as baseline.

options.t: The peak of the R wave, used as the reference for amplitude
options.why: R wave amplitude is measured from the baseline, and it is not called the J point.

options.t: Where the T wave begins, marking the end of the ST segment
options.why: That junction ends the ST segment rather than starting it.

options.t: The lowest point of the S wave, defining QRS depth
options.why: That is simply the nadir of the S wave.

options.t: Where the QRS ends and the ST segment begins

questions.stem: What segment is normally used as the isoelectric baseline for measuring ST deviation?
questions.why: The TP segment is electrically silent, so it defines the true baseline. When the rate is fast enough that TP disappears, the PR segment is used instead.

options.t: The peak of the preceding T wave
options.why: A wave peak is a deflection, not a baseline.

options.t: The ST segment of the preceding complex
options.why: That is the segment being measured; it cannot also be the reference.

options.t: The QT interval averaged across the strip
options.why: The QT is a duration, not a level to measure against.

options.t: The TP segment, before the next P wave

questions.stem: Why is lead II the usual choice for continuous rhythm monitoring?
questions.why: Lead II is oriented roughly along the normal direction of depolarization, so P waves are upright and well defined — exactly what rhythm interpretation depends on. MCL1 is the common alternative when you need to see the QRS shape.

options.t: It is the only lead that displays atrial activity
options.why: Any lead can show P waves; lead II usually shows them best.

options.t: It is least affected by patient movement
options.why: Movement artifact affects the limb leads similarly.

options.t: It runs along the heart's axis, so P waves are clear
It provides the most reliable view of the ST segments
options.why: ST analysis needs a 12-lead; a single monitoring lead is not adequate for it.

questions.stem: Match each part of the tracing to what is happening in the heart.
questions.why: Reading a strip is matching the picture to the electrical event. Everything from block to infarct is a distortion of one of these six.
pairs: Time from atrial depolarization to ventricular depolarization

questions.stem: Match each lead group to the wall of the heart it views.
questions.why: Localizing a STEMI means knowing which leads look where. Contiguous elevation in one group, with reciprocal depression in the opposite group, is the pattern you are hunting.

questions.stem: In a strip where the P waves march out at 300 per minute but only every third one is followed by a QRS, what is the ventricular rate?
questions.why: Divide the atrial rate by the conduction ratio: 300 divided by 3 is 100. Atrial flutter near 300 with variable block is exactly why atrial and ventricular rates are counted separately.

options.why: The atrial rate carries through to the ventricles only when conduction is one-for-one.
Four-to-one conduction of 300 would give 75.
Two-to-one conduction of 300 gives 150; this strip conducts one in three.

questions.stem: A monitor alarms for a rate of 30 and the strip shows a flat line with occasional sharp spikes. The patient is talking to you. What is your first move?
questions.why: Treat the patient, not the monitor. A conscious, talking patient is not in a rate-30 rhythm — check electrode contact, cable connections and lead selection before anything else.

options.t: Print a 12-lead before doing anything else
options.why: A 12-lead is worth having, but a talking patient with a flat monitor line is an equipment problem first.

options.t: Check the leads and the patient rather than the number
Give atropine and prepare for a deteriorating rhythm
options.why: Treating a monitor artifact with a drug does the patient no good.

options.t: Begin transcutaneous pacing for symptomatic bradycardia
options.why: The patient is awake and talking, so nothing on the monitor is being confirmed by the patient.

questions.stem: What are the normal duration and height limits for a P wave?
questions.why: Under 0.11 seconds wide and under 2.5 mm tall. A P that is too tall points to right atrial enlargement, one that is too wide or notched to left atrial enlargement.

options.t: Under 0.20 seconds and under 5 mm
options.why: 0.20 is the PR interval limit; 5 mm is well past a normal P.

options.t: Under 0.12 seconds and under 10 mm
options.why: The height limit is far lower than 10 mm.

options.t: Under 0.04 seconds and under 1 mm
options.why: 0.04 seconds is one small box — the Q wave limit, not the P.

options.t: Under 0.11 seconds and under 2.5 mm

questions.stem: What defines a normal Q wave, as opposed to a pathologic one?
questions.why: One small box wide and no deeper than a third of the QRS. Past either limit it is a pathologic Q, which is the EKG signature of infarction — dead tissue that no longer depolarizes.

options.t: Any Q wave in a limb lead is pathologic
options.why: Small Q waves are normal in several leads.

options.t: Under 0.04 seconds and under one third of the QRS height
Under 0.12 seconds and under half the QRS height
options.why: Both figures are too generous — a Q that size is pathologic.

options.t: Under 0.11 seconds and under 2.5 mm
options.why: Those are the P wave limits, not the Q wave's.

questions.stem: Which description matches a normal T wave?
questions.why: Normal T waves lean — a slow upstroke and a faster downstroke — stay under half the QRS height, and point the same way as the QRS in that lead. Symmetry is the finding that should catch your eye.

options.t: Asymmetric, taller than the QRS, opposite the QRS
options.why: A T taller than the QRS and opposite in direction is abnormal on both counts.

options.t: Asymmetric, under half the QRS height, same direction as the QRS
Symmetric, under half the QRS height, same direction as the QRS
options.why: A symmetric, peaked or pointed T is the abnormal shape.

options.t: Symmetric, with a rounded peak, upright in each lead
options.why: T wave direction follows the QRS, so it is not upright everywhere.

questions.stem: What QT interval range does the lecture give as normal?
questions.why: 390 to 460 ms. A long QT is the setup for torsades de pointes, which is why the interval matters at all in the field.

options.t: 390 to 460 milliseconds
300 to 390 milliseconds
options.why: That range sits below the normal window taught here.

options.t: 460 to 600 milliseconds
options.why: That range is prolonged, which is the finding that precedes torsades.

options.t: 120 to 200 milliseconds
options.why: 0.12 to 0.20 seconds is the PR interval.

questions.stem: A U wave measures more than 2 mm. What does that suggest?
questions.why: A U wave can be normal if small; over 2 mm it is abnormal and points at low potassium or cardiomyopathy. It sits just after the T wave and is easy to mistake for a P.

options.t: Acute inferior infarction
options.why: Infarction shows in ST segments and Q waves rather than the U wave.

options.t: Hyperkalemia
options.why: Hyperkalemia shows as peaked T waves and a widening QRS, not a prominent U.

options.t: Hypokalemia or cardiomyopathy
Digitalis at a therapeutic level
options.why: Digitalis has its own scooped ST appearance rather than a tall U wave.

questions.stem: A patient with a severe headache shows deeply inverted T waves across the tracing. What should this suggest?
questions.why: Deeply inverted T waves — often called cerebral T waves — accompany acute CNS events such as intracranial hemorrhage. The heart is structurally fine; the finding is a clue about the head.

options.t: Lead placement reversed on the limbs
options.why: Reversed limb leads distort specific leads rather than inverting T waves broadly.

options.t: An old myocardial infarction
options.why: An old infarct leaves pathologic Q waves rather than deep symmetric T inversion.

options.t: An acute central nervous system event
Normal variation in a young patient
options.why: Deep inversion across the tracing is not a normal variant.

questions.stem: What does Einthoven's theory state, and which lead gives the best routine view?
questions.why: Every contraction emits electrical energy that surface electrodes can detect. Leads I, II and III are the bipolar leads, each measuring the difference in potential between two electrodes, and lead II usually gives the clearest view.

options.t: Electrical energy is emitted only during repolarization; lead II
options.why: Energy is emitted with contraction — depolarization — not only on repolarization.

options.t: The heart emits electrical energy with each contraction; lead II
The heart's electrical activity is measured only by the precordials; lead V1
options.why: The limb leads measure it too, and V1 is not the routine monitoring lead.

options.t: The heart emits electrical energy with each contraction; lead I
options.why: Lead I is a bipolar lead but not the one named as the best routine view.

questions.stem: What are the five steps of dysrhythmia interpretation in order?
questions.why: Find the P, QRS and T; measure the PR interval — three to five boxes; measure the QRS — 2.5 boxes or less; decide whether the rhythm is regular; then count the rate off a six-second strip times ten.

options.t: Identify the waves, measure rate, assess regularity, measure PRI, measure QRS
options.why: Rate comes after the intervals and regularity in this sequence.

options.t: Assess regularity, measure rate, identify the waves, measure PRI, measure QRS
options.why: The waves are identified first so the intervals have something to measure between.

options.t: Measure rate, identify the waves, measure PRI, measure QRS, assess regularity
options.why: Rate is the last step, not the first.

options.t: Identify the waves, measure PRI, measure QRS, assess regularity, measure rate

questions.stem: What R-R shortcuts does the review sheet give for a rate over 100 and under 60?
questions.why: Three large boxes is 100 per minute and five is 60, so an R-R shorter than three means tachycardia and one longer than five means bradycardia. It is a glance, not a measurement.

options.t: Under 3 small boxes is over 100; over 5 small boxes is under 60
options.why: The shortcut counts large boxes, not small ones.

options.t: Under 5 large boxes is over 100; over 3 large boxes is under 60
options.why: That reverses the two thresholds.

options.t: Under 2 large boxes is over 100; over 6 large boxes is under 60
options.why: Neither figure matches the sheet.

options.t: Under 3 large boxes is over 100; over 5 large boxes is under 60

questions.stem: What distinguishes irregularly irregular from regularly irregular?
questions.why: Irregularly irregular means no two R-R intervals match — atrial fibrillation is the classic. Regularly irregular means the irregularity repeats predictably, as in Wenckebach or a bigeminy pattern.

options.t: Irregularly irregular means the rate varies; regularly irregular means the rate is fixed
options.why: Both describe R-R spacing rather than overall rate.

options.t: Irregularly irregular occurs only in atrial fibrillation; regularly irregular only in flutter
options.why: Both descriptions apply to more than one rhythm.

options.t: Irregularly irregular has no two R-R intervals alike; regularly irregular follows a pattern
Irregularly irregular follows a pattern; regularly irregular does not
options.why: That reverses the two definitions.
